blocks.text: Indian classical music is divided into two categories:
Hindustani music and Carnatic music.
1. Hindustani Music (North India)
Sung in languages: Hindi, Braj, Avadhi, Rajasthani, Marathi.
2, Carnatic Music (South India)
Sung in languages:
Sanskrit, Kannada, Malayalam, Tamil.
Common Elements in Both Traditions
1. Raga: A melodic framework, each associated with a specific emotion or time of the day. E.g. Miyan ki Todi (sung during late morning hours).
2. Taal: A rhythmic framework based on cyclic time units.
3. Sruti: The smallest measurable difference between musical pitches.
7 Basic Swaras in Indian Music (Sargam)

3 Major Vocal Forms of Hindustani Music Dhrupad
It is sung with a Tanpura and Pankhawaj.
Dhrupad was first composed by Miyan Tansen.
It was propounded by Dagar family and Darbhanga Gharana.
A more lyrical and expressive form that evolved from Dhrupad, known for its freedom of expression and romantic themes.
Khayal was first composed by Amir Khusrau.
It is performed towards the end of concert.
It is used to convey the mood of elation.
Tillana of Carnatic music is based on this.
Tighter vocal forms in Hindustani classical music, often considered semi- classical, include Dhamar (associated with Dhrupad), Kajari, Tappa, Thumri, Ghazal, Bhajan, Tripal, and Chaiti.
Major Styles of Carnatic Music
1. Gitam: A simple melodic extension of the raga with a uniform tempo and introductory piece.
2. Svarajati: Mix of devotional and heroic elements. This is learnt after a course of Gitam.
3. Kirtanam: It comprises of devotional songs.
4. Tillana: Short, crisp compositions, similar to Tarana in Hindustani music.
5. Kriti: It comprises of highly evolved musical compositions.
It is a development from Kirtana.
6. Suladi: An extension of raga-based compositions.
7. Padam: A love poem/tempo.

"> Raga-Based Performances:
> Thumri, Dhrupad, and Prabandha are all traditional forms of raga-based performances in Indian classical music.
>Thunri: The thumri is very lyrical in its structure and presentation. Thumri is a love song and hence the textual beauty is very important.
> Sonata is a structural form associated with Western classical music.
"+ Structure of Dhrupad: Dhrupad has four parts and the dhrupad proper is a song in four parts. The four parts of a dhrupad composition (also known as tuks or segments) are:
1. Sthayi (or Asthayi): The base/refrain, covering the lower and middle octaves.
2. Antara: Covers the middle and higher octaves.
3. Sanchari: The development phase, using all three octaves.
4, Abhoga: The concluding section.
+ Raga Vivodha and Pandit Somnath: In the text Raga Vivodha, Pandit Somnath defined a raga through two main components.
> The first is Devamaya Swarupa, which represents the ethos or spiritual/emotional form.
>The second is Nadamaya Swarupa (also known as Swarlakshana), which represents the tonal structure of the raga.
+ Achal and Chal Swaras: In the 7 basic notes, there are two categories of swaras: 'Achal' and 'Chal'.
> Achal Swaras (Fixed): "Sa " and "Pa " are Achal swaras and are always "Shuddha " (pure). They never change position.
> Chal Swaras (Movable): These notes have variants categorized into "Komal" (flat) and "Teevra " (sharp).
All other swaras except sa & pa are Chal Swaras.
" Types of Jati in Rhythm (Carnatic Music): There are 5 main Jatis in the rhythmic structure:
>Tishra Jati (3 beats): A pattern based on three, often performed as 1+2 or 3.

> Chaturashra Jati (4 beats): A pattern based on four, commonly used as the default in many talas (1+3 or > Khanda Jati (5 beats): A pattern based on five (2+3 or > Mishra Jati (7 beats): A pattern based on seven (3+4 or > Sankeerna Jati (9 beats): A pattern based on nine (4+5 or 3+2+4)
"+ Jati in Melodic Structure (Range Classification): In Melodic terms, Particularly within Hindustani music, Jati classifies ragas by the number of notes (Svaras) in their scale:
> Audav jati: Pentatonic scales containing five notes.
> Shadav Jati: Hexatonic scales containing six notes.
> Sampurna Jati: Heptatonic scales containing all seven notes.
> Mixed Jati (Mishra): Combination, such as Audav- Sampurna (5 in aroh, 7 in avroh)
"+ Rhythmic Cycles (Talas): In Indian classical music, the rhythmic cycle is referred to as "Tala ". Few specific Talas and their beats:
> Adi Tala: Consists of 8 beats.
> Mishra Chapu: Consists of 7 beats.
> Rupak Tala: Consists of 3 or 6 beats.
Teentaal:
> Teentaal consists of 16 beats (matras).
> These 16 beats are divided into four sections of four beats each (4-4-4-4).
> A clap (Taali) falls on the Ist, 5th, and 13th beats.
> An empty beat (Khali) falls on the 9th beat.
Saptak Notation System:
> Dot above (S): Taar Saptak (High Octave).
> Dot below (S): Mandra Saptak (Low Octave).
> No dot (S): Madhya Saptak (Middle Octave).
Gamaka:
> Gamaka refers to any graceful turn, curve, or oscillation applied to a single note or between notes.
> The specific type of Gamaka used by gliding from one note to another is called Meend, which is commonly used in Hindustani classical music.
Khayal:
> It is a romantic and highly ornamented style of singing.
>The musical compositions in Khayal are called "Bandish".

It is also famously known as the "Mirror of Gesture ".

> Nritya: Expressive dance (involving emotions and expressions).

Types of Musical Instruments of India In Natya Shastra, Bharat Muni categorizes Indian musical instruments into four main types: Avanaddha (membrano- phones), Ghana (idiophones), Sushira (aerophones), and Tat (chordophones).
Tantu Vadya (Chordophones)— String Instruments Sound is produced by plucking or bowing the stretched strings. E.g., Sitar, Sarod, Santoor, Veena, Rudra Veena, Violin, Surbahar, Guitar, Mohan Veena.
. Sushir Vadya (Aerophones) > Wind Instruments Sound is produced by blowing air through instrument.
E.g., Flute, Shehnai, Nadaswaram.
. Avanaddha Vadya (Membranophones) — Percussion Instruments Sound is produced by striking a stretched membrane (made of animal skin) or drumhead. E.g., Tabla, Pakhawaj, Mridangam, Drums.
Percussion instruments are of two types:
'—2.Membranophones: A membranophone is an instrument which produce sound by a stretched membrane that is struck or vibrated. E.g. Tabla, mridangam, etc.
. Ghana Vadya (Idiophones)—> Solid Instruments Sound is produced by striking or shaking solid materials.
E.g., Ghatam, Manjira, Kartal.
